title: The undeclared
hook: ten questions the Buddha set aside, and why silence was the answer

segments.voice: Yesterday: pathavi, the earth that doesn't recoil from what's thrown on it. Your line: let it land, and stay wide. Today ends a week.

A monk named Māluṅkyāputta is sitting alone, and he's had enough. There are questions the Buddha never answers. Is the world eternal, or not? Is it finite, or infinite? Are the soul and the body the same thing, or different? Does an awakened one exist after death, or not, or both, or neither? Ten questions in all. So he goes to the Buddha with an ultimatum: answer them, or I'm giving up the training and going home. It's the kind of message you type at two in the morning.
screen: `TEN QUESTIONS.` → `ANSWER THEM, OR I LEAVE.` → `AN ULTIMATUM.`

segments.voice: First, the Buddha asks a question of his own. Did I ever promise you, come and train with me and I'll answer these? No. Did you ever say, I'll train only if you do? No. Then who are you, and what are you walking away from? Then comes a picture. Suppose a man is shot with an arrow thickly smeared with poison. His friends bring a surgeon. And the man says: don't pull it out until I know who shot me. Was he a noble, a brahmin, a merchant, a laborer? What was his name, his clan? Tall or short, dark or fair? What village was he from? What kind of bow was it, what was the string made of, and the feathers on the shaft? That man, the Buddha says, would die before he ever found out. So the ten questions stay undeclared, avyākata, not answered either way. Not because they're forbidden, and the sutta doesn't call them meaningless. Because answering them isn't beneficial, he says. It doesn't lead to letting go, to peace, to awakening. And what has he declared? This is suffering. This is its arising. This is its ending. This is the way. Four things, all about pulling the arrow out. The sutta ends with a line worth keeping: remember what I've left undeclared as undeclared, and what I've declared as declared. Buddhist schools have gone on discussing the ten questions. But the silence itself is a teaching. Some questions you can carry for a lifetime without letting them stop you walking.
screen: `DID I EVER PROMISE YOU THAT?` · `THE POISONED ARROW.` · `NOT BENEFICIAL, NOT LEADING TO PEACE.` · `FOUR THINGS DECLARED.` · then, large: `THE UNDECLARED.`

segments.voice: Let one big question come up, one you've chewed on, why something happened, what comes after, whether you chose right, and name it once, gently. Instead of answering, set it down beside you like a closed book and return to the breath. When it taps your shoulder, notice it and come back; it can stay undeclared for now.
The undeclared. Ten questions the Buddha set aside, because answering them doesn't pull the arrow out.
Your line: pull the arrow out. And that's week sixty-five: kukkura, Abhaya, how many feelings, apannaka, before, the earth, and the undeclared. Day four hundred fifty-five.
screen: `WEEK SIXTY-FIVE: DOG-DUTY · TRAP QUESTION · FEELINGS · SAFE BET · BEFORE · EARTH · UNDECLARED`

howItsDone: Some Buddhist teachers tell the parable of the poisoned arrow to students who want metaphysical questions settled first, and the ten undeclared questions come up in commentaries and debates across schools.

original.note: Pali avyākata (also spelled abyākata): undeclared, left unexplained.

trapdoor: what you thought: the undeclared means the Buddha didn't know.
what it means: ten questions deliberately set aside, because answering them doesn't lead to peace.
what a scholar hears: MN 63, the Cūḷamāluṅkya Sutta; the same ten questions recur across the canon, and Buddhist schools have debated why they were left unanswered.
recall: the tree whose leaves the Buddha held

chat.says: Why didn't the Buddha just answer whether the world is eternal?
options: It doesn't help: like a man with a poisoned arrow, pull it out first.
He didn't know the answer, so he changed the subject instead.
Those questions are forbidden, and asking them is a sin.
chat.meaning: In MN 63 the Buddha leaves ten questions undeclared because answering them doesn't lead to peace or awakening. He declares suffering, its arising, its ending, the way.

Māluṅkyāputta.meaning: a monk who demanded answers to ten questions

brahmin.meaning: a member of the priestly class in old India

Abhaya.meaning: the prince who brought the trap question
